svg.title: How a damping ring makes a beam narrower
svg.desc: Drawing in two parts. Above, a ring of pipe seen at an angle, with five blue bending magnets, a grey cavity and a short wiggler. A wide, fuzzy beam of particles, labelled beam in, joins the ring at the upper left. The beam runs round the ring clockwise, and arrows in the middle say thousands of turns. Copper coloured light flies off forwards at every bending magnet. A thin, sharp beam, labelled beam out, leaves the ring at the lower left. Four numbered notes above the drawing are matched by numbers on it. 1 The beam goes in wide. 2 Every bend makes it give off light, which takes away a little of all its motion, the sideways part too. 3 A cavity pushes it on, only forwards. 4 The sideways motion is never given back, so after thousands of turns the beam comes out narrow, at a steady size. Below, on a dark panel, a close view of the wiggler. Two rows of magnet blocks, one above the beam and one below, with north and south poles alternating along each row and opposite poles facing each other. Between the rows lies a flat sheet, and on it the beam follows a wave from side to side, drawn exaggerated. A bright point marks every bend, and copper coloured light leaves each one forwards. In the EPITA project these magnets are permanent and need no electric current.
